Existing problems with intercultural relations may be attributed to events which have occurred between members of the two cultures during the past seventy years. Upon examination of these events, and considering recent trends, these relationships appear to be heading for improvement.
In 1904 Congress passed Public Law 183 (33 Stat. 352) opening 1.1 million acres of the Crow Ceded Area to non-Indian homesteaders. The resulting influx naturally created cultural and social problems, especially since there were pressures for additional reductions of reservation lands.
Then in 1937, Public Law 410 (50 Stat. 884) eliminated the Hardin area from within the reservation boundaries. This act has caused resentment for a number of reasons, one being that the Crow Tribe received no compensation for the loss of lands. This act allowed Hardin businessmen to sell alcoholic beverages (although not to Indians). Hardin, less than a mile from the Crow Reservation, subsequently became the primary source of "boot-leg" liquor for Indians. Over the years alcoholism and problems related to alcohol consumption have become the greatest social disease among the Crows — perhaps the single most important factor which has further broken down cultural strength and led to additional land losses.
As mentioned earlier, the existing intercultural conflicts generally stem from disagreements over ownership and control of reservation lands. These problems began earlier in the century and were intensified when alcoholic beverages became more readily available in 1937.
